sections.bio:
Most businesses treat LinkedIn like a billboard.
I help them turn it into a system.

Over the last few years, I've worked with 30+ founders, CEOs, and CXOs, helping them:
- Build LinkedIn profiles that attract the right buyers
- Create content that drives inbound enquiries, not just impressions
- Run lead generation frameworks tailored to B2B sales cycles
- Optimize for SEO so the right people find them organically
- Automate backend growth workflows using AI tools

The result: predictable attention from decision-makers, without running ads or doing cold outreach the wrong way.

Here is what I actually do:
→ LinkedIn Growth: Profile optimization, content strategy, ghostwriting, and lead generation systems
→ SEO: On-page and off-page optimization built for organic lead flow
→ Web Development: Clean, conversion-focused websites and landing pages
→ AI Automation: Workflow automation for marketing and business operations
→Social Media Management: Full-stack management across LinkedIn and other platforms

I also bring project management experience in cross-functional marketing campaigns, from strategy to execution, working with founders, international clients, and distributed teams.

If you are a founder or business looking to grow: DM me or check the Featured section.

posts.text:
the people closest to me think i am wasting money on where i live.


the rent here costs noticeably more than it would in a dozen other pockets of the city, and from a distance it does look like an easy number to cut, the kind of expense people assume you would drop the moment you needed to save.
but i have started to see it differently, not as rent, but as an entry fee into a certain kind of room.

since moving here, i have started noticing things i never paid attention to before, the gym at six in the morning is somehow already full, the lift conversations are about term sheets and deadlines instead of small talk, the neighbour two doors down is building something at thirty that most people would not attempt at fifty. none of it is performative, it is just what normal looks like in this particular pocket of the city.

you do not absorb a mindset from a book you read once, you absorb it from what becomes normal around you, from watching a certain standard of living and thinking actually being lived by people close enough to observe, instead of only reading about it from far away.

there is also the version of this that has nothing to do with mindset at all, the facilities that simply make the actual work easier, a workspace that functions, a building that does not require half your energy just to operate around it. some of what you pay for here is not inspiration, it is just fewer daily obstacles between you and the thing you are trying to build.

i did not move here for the address. i moved here because i wanted proof, every single day, that a certain kind of ambition was possible and already being lived out by people around me, not just something i had read about somewhere else.
when your environment raises what feels normal to you, you stop negotiating with yourself about whether bigger goals are realistic, because you are surrounded by people for whom they already are.

so no, i do not think i am wasting money.

i think i am paying to keep good company, good manners, and good ambition within arm's reach of my everyday life, and that is not an expense, that is the actual investment.

i recommend leaving your parents house! 

not because anything is wrong with staying there, if anything it is probably the most comfortable version of life you will ever have, which is exactly why staying too long in it becomes a problem nobody really warns you about.

comfort has a way of deciding your ambition for you if you let it sit long enough. everything is already taken care of at home, rent does not exist as a concept you have to think about, groceries appear, bills get paid somewhere upstream of your daily life, and none of it requires you to actually understand what any of it costs.

the first month on my own, i sat with my first real set of bills laid out in front of me, rent, electricity, groceries, the help that used to just be part of the house growing up, wifi, and it hit me that none of it had ever actually been free, it had simply never been mine to notice before.

what nobody really prepares you for is not the cost itself, it is the standard you refuse to let go of. i did not want a smaller version of the life i grew up with, i wanted the exact same one, just now funded entirely by me, and that gap between what i was used to and what i could actually afford on my own became the thing that pushed me harder than almost anything else has.

you start finding ways. you take on the extra project, you negotiate the rate you would have accepted without a second thought a year earlier, you stop treating comfort as something that gets handed to you and start treating it as something you build, expense by expense, in exactly the shape you already knew you wanted.

leaving was never really about the house. it was about the moment your standard of living stops being inherited and starts being something you have to earn on your own terms.

nobody tells you that growing up mostly just means paying, out of your own pocket, for the version of comfort you already got used to for free.

your work is an acquired taste, the same way dimsum is.
not everyone who tries it will like it, and that has nothing to do with how good it is.

some people love it on the first bite. some take a few tries before it clicks. some never come around to it no matter how many times they try, and none of that says anything about the dimsum itself, it is simply how taste works.

the place making it does not change the recipe every time someone does not immediately like it. it keeps making it exactly the way it is meant to be made, and the people it is meant for eventually find their way to it anyway.

your work follows the same rule, whether you write, design, consult, or build anything that carries a point of view.

early on, i took on almost every client who reached out, mostly out of fear that turning anyone away meant fewer opportunities later. i softened my actual point of view on calls just to sound like a safer, more agreeable fit for whoever was sitting across from me.

it rarely worked. the clients i shaped myself to please almost never stayed long, because i was not really working with them, i was performing a version of myself i thought they wanted, and that version cannot hold up over months of actual work together.

you do not have to work with every client who comes your way.

that is exactly how you end up working with the ones who actually value it, long term. the ones who never needed convincing, who got what you do without you having to shrink it down first.

develop the acquired taste. stop trying to be liked by everyone who walks past it.

for the first year of doing this, i replied to every client message the second it came in, whatever time it was, whatever day it was, because i was scared that any delay would look unprofessional.

one client in particular would message anytime between eight in the morning and midnight, sometimes about the actual post, sometimes just an idea he had in the shower, and for months i answered every single one within minutes because i thought that was the whole job.

it caught up with me eventually. i was tired in a way that had nothing to do with the actual work and everything to do with never switching off, and the quality of my thinking started dropping because i was reacting all day instead of sitting with anything long enough to do it properly.

so i changed one thing. i told him i would check messages twice a day, morning and evening, and that anything genuinely urgent could go through a call instead of sitting in a message for hours.

i expected pushback. what i got was relief. he did not need instant replies either, he had just never been offered another option, and once the boundary existed he started sending fewer, more thought through messages instead of scattered ones all day.

that is when client handling actually made sense to me. it has very little to do with being available every hour and a lot to do with being dependable at the hours you said you would be there.

the clients who seem to test your boundaries were rarely testing anything, they were just working the way everyone works until someone shows them a better way.

set the boundary before you resent someone for something they were never told not to do.

I have started spending more time lately in rooms i used to only see from outside, five star lobbies, offices that make my first laptop look like a toy, and it has completely changed what i thought success looked like day to day.

i expected the busiest people in the room. what i actually find is the calmest. the founders and ceos i sit across from take their time before answering anything, do not reach for their phone the second there is a silence, and will spend twenty unhurried minutes on one decision instead of rushing through ten of them badly.

on one call, someone who runs a company most people in this city would recognise instantly listened for almost the entire hour, asked two sharp questions, said "let us do this," and walked out for lunch. no follow up meeting, no five people looped in, no packed calendar waiting on the other side of it.

that is when it landed for me. the busy, always-on version of working hard is not what success looks like up close, it is usually what being early in your career looks like. the people who have actually made it protect their time like it never comes back, say no far more often than yes, and let long uninterrupted stretches do the thinking the rest of us try to force through hours logged.

working less was never the actual goal. working on fewer things with your full attention is, and that is a completely different skill.
